I'm going to pass on a tip I got a couple years ago that has changed everything in my tomato preserving game, but please don't think I'm knocking this accomplishment AT ALL.

The tip is: only can tomato PASTE, not sauce.

The reasoning behind that advice is that paste is so much quicker to prepare than sauce is (not an insignificant plus when you've got a ton of garden produce to process in a short time window) and that it also takes up so much less pantry space, requires less expensive smaller jars and so on. It's so easy to throw together your great pasta sauce recipes with home canned tomato paste that the space and time savings when you are drowning in garden tomatoes is totally worth it. Do what you will with that advice, making stuff from scratch is so rewarding whatever method you choose, and obviously home made pasta sauce makes a much better gift than tomato paste lol :)

How do you make and can paste?

Oh man, there are a million ways. This is the most basic and a good place to start: https://www.almanac.com/canned-tomato-sauce

Start with a good meaty paste tomato variety.

Wash them, then core them (remove the stem and the thick white part that goes into the tomato a bit - there is a tool called a tomato corer that makes this super quick) dip them whole into a pot of boiling water for about 10-30 seconds until the skins split then use a slotted spoon to move them to a bowl of ice water to stop them from cooking. Mash them up through a sieve to remove all the seeds (a food mill does this in one quick step) put the tomato mash on a stove or in a slow cooker for a few hours until the excess liquid has evaporated and you have the consistency you want. Add a splash of lemon juice and then follow the instructions that came with your canner.

Start off small and work your way up. Start with only a few common hardier/easier varieties such as tomatoes, peppers, onions, and squash. That'll be enough to learn the basics, and the following year consider adding a few more varieties.

Start at the soil and your plants will do the rest. Look for small farms that have a few horses/cattle/sheep that you can get manure free/cheap. Compost the manure first, or add it in the fall to decompose naturally, but don't add fresh stuff to your plants.

Healthy soil takes time to build by using tons of organic matter over the years. If you keep adding a couple inches of woodchips and compost every year, it'll build up over time and make a fantastic soil.

If you live in a more urban area, your topsoil was probably stripped off and sold, leaving the poor soil underneath that lacks organic matter. Without this, you'll have trouble growing plants regardless of what fertilizer you use. If you live in a rural area, it might have too much clay or sand. In any case, compost/manure will help. Even thick woodchips break down over time, and small woodchips even faster.
